facts.claim: Rudolf Bayer and Edward McCreight introduced the B-tree in “Organization and maintenance of large ordered indexes” (Acta Informatica, 1972).
Use The Index, Luke: tree depth grows very slowly compared to the number of leaf nodes; real-world indexes with millions of records have a depth of four or five.
Use The Index, Luke: the number of indexes on a table is the most dominant factor for insert performance, and each additional index slows inserts further.
Use The Index, Luke: a database can use a two-column index when searching by its leading column, but not by the second column alone, like a telephone directory.
PostgreSQL’s planner estimates each plan’s cost, in arbitrary units, and seeks the lowest estimated total cost; EXPLAIN shows its estimated rows.
PostgreSQL’s docs: fetching rows one at a time costs much more than reading them in order, and a table on one page nearly always gets a full scan, indexes or not.
PostgreSQL’s docs: a nested-loop join runs its lookup into the second table once for each row of the first, and that lookup can go through an index.
SQLite’s docs (checked 2026-10-30): a full table scan reads the whole table to find one row, so its time grows in step with the number of rows.
PostgreSQL’s docs (checked 2026-10-30): every table and index is stored as pages of one fixed size, usually 8 kB, and a row can sit on any page.
PostgreSQL’s docs (checked 2026-10-30): by default its planner counts a page fetched out of order as 4 times the cost of a page read in order.
PostgreSQL’s docs (checked 2026-10-30): the database must keep every index in step with its table, which adds work to every write, so indexes seldom or never used should be removed.
